quality.title: CV check
quality.clean: Nothing to flag. The CV looks tidy.
quality.countErrors: {count, plural, =1 {1 thing to fix} other {# things to fix}}
quality.countWarnings: {count, plural, =1 {1 to look at} other {# to look at}}
quality.nationalId: This looks like a national identity number in the CV. Take it out — employers never need it, and it is what identity theft is built on.
quality.noName: The CV has no name on it.
quality.noContact: Nobody can reach you. Add an email address or a phone number.
quality.emailLooksWrong: That email address does not look right. Check it before you send anything.
quality.noTitle: Without a title the reader has to guess what you are applying for. Write something like “Frontend developer” or “Nurse”.
quality.noCity: Add a town or city. Employers often sort by where you are.
quality.linkNotAUrl: “{label}” is not a working link. It has to start with https:// to be clickable in the PDF.
quality.noHistory: The CV has no jobs and no education yet.
quality.noSummary: The summary is empty. Two to four sentences at the top is the one part a reader is certain to read.
quality.summaryShort: The summary is very short. Say what you do, for how long, and what you are good at.
quality.summaryLong: The summary is long. It is read first and should be two to four sentences.
quality.entryNoDates: “{entry}” has no dates. A hole in the timeline reads as something being hidden.
quality.entryInFuture: “{entry}” starts in the future. Is that date right?
quality.gap: There is a {months}-month gap in the timeline. That is fine — but expect to be asked, and consider explaining it in the summary.
quality.tooManyBullets: “{entry}” has {count} bullets. Three to five is enough; the best ones get read and the rest get skimmed.
quality.longBullet: A bullet under “{entry}” is long enough to be skipped. One line each.
quality.referencesOnRequest: You are listing contact details for {count, plural, =1 {one reference} other {# references}}. Many people write “References available on request” instead — and ask the person first either way.
quality.photo: The CV has a photo. That is normal in Norway but not required, and some employers ask for one without to avoid bias.
quality.tooLong: The CV runs to {pages} pages. Two is the usual ceiling; under ten years of experience, one is plenty.
quality.letterEmpty: The cover letter is switched on but empty. It goes out as the first page of the PDF.
quality.letterLong: The cover letter is long enough to run past one page. Three or four paragraphs is the norm.
quality.letterNoPosition: The cover letter does not say which job it is for. That is the first thing a reader looks for.

help.personalia:
Your name, a title, and one way to reach you.
The title is read first. Write the job you are applying for, not the one you have.
Skip national ID numbers and street addresses. A town is enough.
help.photo:
Common in Norway, but never required.
Use a plain daylight portrait.
If an employer asks for a CV without a photo, switch it off here.
help.summary:
Two to four sentences: what you do, for how long, and what you are good at.
Be concrete. "Frontend developer with eight years in finance" beats "structured and solution-oriented".
help.experience:
Most recent job first.
Two to four bullets about what you achieved.
Write results, not duties: "cut load time by 42%" beats "responsible for performance".
help.education:
Most recent first: degree, institution and years.
Just graduated? Add relevant courses, grades or your thesis title.
help.skills:
What you could use at work tomorrow.
Five to twelve is enough. Thirty says nothing is important.
Be honest about levels. You may be asked in the interview.
help.languages:
Languages and level.
Include a language when your level is worth showing.
help.certifications:
Certification, issuer and date.
Only what is relevant and still valid.
help.projects:
Projects that show something your jobs do not.
Add a link if there is something to look at.
help.courses: Only courses relevant to the role.
help.volunteering:
Volunteering counts as experience.
Especially when it shows responsibility or leadership.
help.interests:
Three to five, specific.
"Cross-country skiing" starts a conversation. "Music and film" does not.
help.drivingLicence: Include a licence when the job might need one.
help.references:
"References available on request" is normal in Norway.
If you list them: ask the person first, and check the number.
help.custom:
For what fits nowhere else: board roles, publications, awards.
Give it a name an employer understands at once.
help.coverLetter:
One page, three or four paragraphs.
Open with the job, and why that one.
Middle: two or three things you have done that match what they ask for. Explain the CV, do not repeat it.
Close by saying you would be glad to come in.
